# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

On a hot August afternoon, the difference between standing on a tree-lined street and standing on an asphalt parking lot can be fifteen degrees Fahrenheit. This is not a metaphor. It is a measurable, well-documented feature of urban life, and it reveals something important: heat in cities is not distributed equally. It is designed—by choices made decades ago about where to plant trees, what materials to build with, how wide to make streets, and who gets to live where. If heat is designed, then it can be redesigned. Cities have more tools to make summer bearable than most residents realize, but every tool involves tradeoffs, and the politics of those tradeoffs are often harder than the engineering.

## The Urban Heat Island, and Why It Discriminates

Cities run hotter than their surroundings because of the urban heat island effect. Buildings, roads, and parking lots absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, keeping urban temperatures several degrees above those of nearby rural areas. Dark asphalt and concrete have high thermal mass; they soak up heat like a battery.
